claims.text: The starting ZrB2 powders contain native oxide impurities.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C to achieve near-full densification.
A low concentration of boron carbide is to be added to the ZrB2 powder before sintering.
Boron carbide reacts with oxide impurities in borides and removes them by forming more volatile species.
Reaction of boron carbide with interfacial oxide impurities produces a transient liquid phase at ZrB2 grain boundaries.
The transient liquid phase enhances mass transport during sintering.
Boron carbide enables full densification of ZrB2 at approximately 2100–2200 °C under ambient pressure.
Rapid heating and transient-liquid-assisted densification reduce the required high-temperature dwell time.
The proposed processing route minimizes pore formation and growth.
Pores act as initiation sites for corrosion or failure during liquid-plating exposure.
Boron-carbide-modified ZrB2 will have significantly lower porosity than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Boron-carbide-modified ZrB2 will have improved mechanical strength relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Boron-carbide-modified ZrB2 will resist degradation during long-duration liquid-plating exposure better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 often contains entrapped porosity and structural weaknesses.
Entrapped porosity and structural weaknesses in conventional ZrB2 facilitate hole formation and eventual failure during prolonged liquid-plating exposure.
Excessive boron carbide or additive-related porosity may fail to improve hardness and may compromise mechanical properties.
Reaction products may introduce secondary phases or residual porosity if processing is not tightly controlled.
